Research supports normalized linear fusion, but offers no universal coefficient grid for neural–transition hybrids. [Bruch et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.11934) found a single-weight convex combination effective and sample-efficient in hybrid text retrieval; transfer to sequential recommendation remains an empirical question. Category-specific z-score or min–max normalization can address scale differences; estimate and freeze statistics using training-only reference scores so inference does not depend on candidate composition. [Temperature scaling](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/guo17a.html) supports probability calibration, although its evidence concerns classification, not HR@10. Positive temperature scaling preserves standalone rankings but changes a component’s influence in fusion; jointly tuning temperature and residual weight introduces redundant scale freedom.

A reproducible proposal—not a literature-established optimum—is s=(1−α)z_neural+αz_transition with α∈{0,.1,.25,.5,.75,1}, category-specific frozen normalization, and one shared α selected by four-category macro HR@10. Prespecify smoothing, transition-score transformation, checkpoint policy, trial count, and ties favoring smaller α. Dirichlet/backoff smoothing has established support for sparse probability estimates in [language-model retrieval](https://www.iro.umontreal.ca/~nie/IFT6255/zhai-lafferty.pdf); applying it to item transitions is an adaptation. Avoid searching separate category weights unless that additional flexibility is declared beforehand.

With 200 users/category, one changed hit shifts category HR by .005 and macro HR by .00125. Fixed negatives enable paired comparisons but do not eliminate selection optimism. [Dwork et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629) explain adaptive holdout overfitting: a fixed small search reduces adaptivity, without making the winning validation estimate unbiased. Count checkpoint and architecture choices too. Preserve the host protocol: [Krichene and Rendle](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/651) show sampled ranking metrics can disagree with full-catalog rankings, so 99-negative HR@10 cannot establish full-catalog recommendation quality.
